title: Joel 1:1–12
context: The book opens as “the LORD’s word that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel” (1:1). Joel gives no king’s reign or date, so readers place him in different periods, and these notes leave the setting open. The prophet calls elders and all the land to hear of an unprecedented locust plague, to tell it to their children, and to lament (1:2–12). Four names for locusts appear in 1:4; readers take them as stages of one insect or as different kinds. Drunkards lose their wine, priests lose the offerings, and farmers lose the harvest; even the land mourns. In 1:6–7 the voice speaks of “my land” and “my vine,” which may be the LORD speaking through the prophet or the prophet speaking for the people. Locust plagues were among the covenant warnings (compare Deuteronomy 28:38–39). Shared ground: both traditions read the scene as real devastation that calls the whole community to lament before God, and both include historical, typological, and future readings of it.

verses.text: The LORD’s word that came to Joel, the son of Pethuel.
verses.arminianNotes: The book begins by naming its source: the LORD’s word that came to Joel, son of Pethuel. Arminian readers note that the prophet is a real person addressed by God, whose message calls a community to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the superscription grounding the whole book in divine revelation. Shared ground: both traditions read the opening as establishing Joel’s authority, though little else is known about the prophet or his date.

verses.text: Hear this, you elders, and listen, all you inhabitants of the land! Has this ever happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers?
verses.arminianNotes: Joel calls elders and all inhabitants to hear and asks whether such a thing ever happened before. Arminian readers see the rhetorical question waking a community to the seriousness of the moment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal to elders as a call to those responsible for leading the people. Both traditions read the question as stressing that this disaster is without precedent in living memory, and as a summons to attention.

verses.text: Tell your children about it, and have your children tell their children, and their children, another generation.
verses.arminianNotes: The people are told to tell their children, and their children’s children, about this disaster. Arminian readers see the generations called to remember, so that later ones learn from what happened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the covenant pattern of passing God’s works from generation to generation, compare Psalm 78:4–6 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as calling families to keep memory alive, even memory of judgment.

verses.text: What the swarming locust has left, the great locust has eaten. What the great locust has left, the grasshopper has eaten. What the grasshopper has left, the caterpillar has eaten.
verses.arminianNotes: Four kinds of locust, swarming, great, grasshopper, and caterpillar, eat what each leaves behind. Arminian readers see total devastation described by layering destruction upon destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the four terms may describe stages of one insect or different kinds. Both traditions read the verse as describing complete loss, and they hold the precise identification of the four names openly.

verses.text: Wake up, you drunkards, and weep! Wail, all you drinkers of wine, because of the sweet wine, for it is cut off from your mouth.
verses.arminianNotes: Joel calls drunkards to wake and weep, because the sweet wine is cut off. Arminian readers see a pointed call to those absorbed in pleasure, now confronted with sudden loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse exposing complacency, as those who lived for wine find it gone. Shared ground: both traditions read the call as waking people from indulgence to sorrow and reflection before God.

verses.text: For a nation has come up on my land, strong, and without number. His teeth are the teeth of a lion, and he has the fangs of a lioness.
verses.arminianNotes: A nation has come up on my land, strong and numberless, with teeth like a lion’s. Arminian readers note that the locusts are described as an invading nation, a vivid image of their power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the phrase my land may be the LORD’s own voice through the prophet, stressing that the land belongs to God. Both traditions read the image as portraying the locust swarm with the language of warfare, and they leave open whose voice says my land.

verses.text: He has laid my vine waste, and stripped my fig tree. He has stripped its bark, and thrown it away. Its branches are made white.
verses.arminianNotes: The invader has laid waste my vine and stripped my fig tree, leaving branches white. Arminian readers see the destruction of vine and fig, symbols of peace and plenty in Israel.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as signaling the loss of covenant blessing, compare Micah 4:4 by reference. Shared ground: both traditions read the stripped trees as a picture of complete devastation reaching the most cherished produce of the land.

verses.text: Mourn like a virgin dressed in sackcloth for the husband of her youth!
verses.arminianNotes: Joel calls the land to mourn like a virgin in sackcloth for the husband of her youth. Arminian readers see grief at its deepest, the sorrow of a young bride bereaved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image as expressing the depth of loss the community should feel. Both traditions read the comparison soberly, as a call to lament proportionate to the disaster, without overreading its details.

verses.text: The meal offering and the drink offering are cut off from the LORD’s house. The priests, the LORD’s ministers, mourn.
verses.arminianNotes: The meal and drink offerings are cut off from the LORD’s house, and the priests mourn. Arminian readers see that the disaster reaches worship itself, interrupting the people’s daily offerings to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loss of offerings as especially grievous, since worship is the heart of covenant life. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing how deeply the plague has struck, cutting off even the means of honoring God.

verses.text: The field is laid waste. The land mourns, for the grain is destroyed, The new wine has dried up, and the oil languishes.
verses.arminianNotes: The field is laid waste and the land mourns, for grain, new wine, and oil fail. Arminian readers see the land itself personified as grieving, sharing the people’s loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that grain, wine, and oil are the basic gifts of covenant blessing, compare Deuteronomy 7:13 by reference. Both traditions read the failure of these staples as a sign that blessing has been withdrawn.

verses.text: Be confounded, you farmers! Wail, you vineyard keepers, for the wheat and for the barley; for the harvest of the field has perished.
verses.arminianNotes: Farmers and vineyard keepers are told to be confounded and wail, for wheat, barley, and harvest have perished. Arminian readers see the human cost of the disaster in those whose livelihood depends on the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see every class of worker called to lament together. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse with compassion for those who have lost their labor and their food.

verses.text: The vine has dried up, and the fig tree withered— the pomegranate tree, the palm tree also, and the apple tree, even all of the trees of the field are withered; for joy has withered away from the sons of men.
verses.arminianNotes: Vine, fig, pomegranate, palm, and apple trees wither, and joy withers away from people. Arminian readers see the inner effect of outer loss: when the land fails, gladness fails too.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse linking the land’s barrenness to the loss of joy that only God’s blessing gives. Both traditions read the closing line as the emotional summit of the unit, a community emptied of gladness.
